newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia sees end to wage arrears nightmare.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia sees end to wage arrears nightmare.

text.p: Russia set an ambitious deadline on Wednesday for paying off massive wage arrears to public-sector workers in a sign the reformist cabinet was gaining confidence about its chances of funding economic reforms.

First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov said Russia would pay off 5.4 trillion roubles ($939 million) in back wages to the military by September and a whopping 25 trillion roubles ($4.3 billion) in other public sector arrears by the end of the year.

The pledges are a strong sign the government is prepared to tackle one of the most serious threats to economic reforms and political stability -- low tax collection rates which make it tough for the state to pay soldiers, teachers and other disgruntled public sector employees.
But economists, noting officials had not given full details on how they would raise the money, said the government could face problems translating its words into deeds.
"There is no doubt the reformists are in charge," said Anthony Thomas, emerging markets analyst at Kleinwort Benson. "I've no doubt they understand what needs to be done. The task is in doing it."

The payoff schedule came after the market-minded cabinet, which also includes golden reformer First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, forced President Boris Yeltsin to make an embarrasing public retraction and scrap his overly ambitious arrears-payment schedule for a more realistic one.

Yeltsin had originally wanted all arrears paid by October 1 but Nemtsov, speaking at a news conference closed to foreign journalists but taped for distribution, said the Kremlin leader had signed a decree on the new, year-end schedule.
"It's a tightening of the timetable and I don't think there's any doubt it will be difficult," said a Western economist, who asked not to be named.
"But that's not to say it's not achievable."

The cabinet, emboldened by its recent success in making some of Russia's most powerful companies cough up billions of dollars in overdue tax payments, has been seeking innovative ways to raise cash to avoid an economic meltdown.

Nemtsov said Yeltsin had signed a decree scrapping oil exports for state needs, a Soviet-era relic which made mountains of money for a few privileged companies which Moscow then often spent on non-urgent items like Kremlin decoration.
Nemtsov said abolishing the scheme would let Russian oil producers pay the equivalent of $521 million in tax arrears to the budget by the end of the year.
